summary: Colloidal silver (silver colloid) is a suspension of tiny silver particles in liquid that is marketed - improperly - as an antimicrobial and immune-boosting product. It is NOT an FDA-approved drug. In a final rule effective September 1999, the FDA determined that all over-the-counter drug products containing colloidal silver ingredients or silver salts (for internal or external use) are NOT generally recognized as safe and effective (not GRASE) and are misbranded. There are NO FDA-approved indications and no proven clinical benefit for the marketed oral/topical colloidal silver products; the strongest published positions (FDA, NIH/NCCIH) conclude the evidence does not support safety or efficacy. The most characteristic harm is ARGYRIA - a permanent blue-grey discoloration of the skin, nails, and mucous membranes that is not reversible. Other reported risks include neurological problems and kidney/liver effects, and silver can interfere with absorption of some medications. Products are nonetheless still sold as dietary supplements; consumers should be counseled honestly that there is no recognized therapeutic role and a real risk of permanent harm.
indications: NONE that are FDA-approved - there is no recognized safe and effective indication for colloidal silver as a drug
Marketed (without FDA recognition or supporting evidence) as a general antimicrobial, cold/flu remedy, and immune supplement - these uses are NOT proven and NOT endorsed
Note: distinct, separately regulated silver-containing prescription products exist (e.g., silver sulfadiazine cream for burns); this record concerns marketed colloidal silver supplements only

dosage.d: No established or FDA-approved therapeutic dose; internal use is not recommended
dosage.n: FDA: not generally recognized as safe and effective; cumulative silver intake raises argyria risk

admin: There is no recognized medical administration; colloidal silver is not an approved drug
Internal (oral) use is discouraged because of cumulative silver deposition and risk of irreversible argyria
If a patient is using a product, document the amount/duration and counsel on stopping and on argyria risk
Do not substitute colloidal silver for proven antimicrobial therapy
moa: Silver ions can nonspecifically bind microbial proteins, enzymes, and nucleic acids, producing in vitro antibacterial effects (the basis for legitimate, separately regulated topical silver products such as silver sulfadiazine and silver dressings). However, for marketed colloidal silver supplements taken internally, no clinically meaningful or FDA-recognized therapeutic mechanism has been established, and systemic absorption leads to deposition of silver in skin and tissues (argyria) rather than a proven therapeutic benefit.

absolute: Use as a substitute for proven, indicated antimicrobial or other medical therapy
relative: Pregnancy and breastfeeding (no safety data; silver crosses placenta and accumulates)
Pre-existing renal or hepatic impairment (tissue deposition)
Concurrent use with medications whose absorption silver may impair (e.g., certain antibiotics, levothyroxine)
monitor: Skin, nail, and mucosal color changes (early argyria)
Renal and hepatic function if chronic ingestion is suspected

preg: Avoid. There are no adequate safety data; silver can cross the placenta and accumulate in tissues, and there is no proven benefit to justify any risk.
lact: Avoid. Safety during breastfeeding has not been established and there is no proven benefit; do not use.
renal: Avoid. Silver can deposit in the kidney and other tissues; renal effects have been reported with chronic ingestion. There is no approved dosing and no benefit to offset the risk.
hepatic: Avoid. Silver deposition in the liver has been reported with chronic exposure. No approved dosing exists and there is no demonstrated benefit.

May reduce absorption of levothyroxine and penicillamine

minor: Interaction data are limited because the product is unregulated as a drug
interactions.food: No established therapeutic food interaction; product is not a recognized drug.
interactions.diagnostics: Chronic silver accumulation can cause skin discoloration that may be mistaken for cyanosis; report use to clinicians.

Argyrosis - blue-grey discoloration of the eyes/conjunctiva

Possible kidney and liver injury with chronic exposure

Otherwise, harms are typically chronic/cumulative rather than acute

counsel: Colloidal silver is NOT an FDA-approved medicine and is not recognized as safe or effective; it is sold only as a supplement
It can cause argyria - a permanent blue-grey discoloration of the skin and eyes that does not go away even after stopping
It does not replace proven treatments; do not delay needed antibiotics or other care
It can interfere with absorption of some medicines (such as certain antibiotics and thyroid medication)
Talk with your clinician before using any silver product, especially if pregnant, breastfeeding, or giving it to a child

pearls: FDA POSITION: Under the FDA final rule effective September 1999 (Federal Register, Aug 17, 1999), all OTC drug products containing colloidal silver ingredients or silver salts are NOT generally recognized as safe and effective (not GRASE) and are misbranded
Regulatory status: not an FDA-approved drug; still sold improperly as a dietary supplement - source for this record is the FDA final rule and NIH/NCCIH consumer guidance, not a drug label
ARGYRIA is the signature toxicity: irreversible blue-grey discoloration of skin, nails, and mucosa; it does not resolve after discontinuation
No proven efficacy as an antimicrobial or immune product when taken internally - do not let patients substitute it for indicated therapy
Distinct from legitimate, separately regulated topical silver products (e.g., silver sulfadiazine, silver wound dressings) - do not conflate them
missed: Not applicable - there is no recommended dosing schedule because colloidal silver has no FDA-approved therapeutic use.
overdose: Acute single-dose toxicity is uncommon; the principal harm is chronic, cumulative argyria (permanent blue-grey discoloration) and possible neurological, renal, or hepatic effects. There is no specific antidote and argyria is not reversible. In suspected ingestion or any acute reaction, provide supportive care and contact a poison control center (1-800-222-1222 in the U.S.).
